mechanism_chain.to: organizational form (ownership, plant scale, contracting, bargaining coverage)
mechanism_chain.link: Legacy technologies were built under the regulated utility model with internal labor markets and denser collective bargaining; wind and solar are more often owned by independent, project-financed producers with small operations staffs.
Rent sharing, bargaining power and internal wage norms raise pay for equally classified workers in legacy plants (relational pay-setting).
Institutional protections matter most for manual/craft occupations and adjust slowly, so gaps concentrate in blue-collar jobs and persist despite employment growth.

hypotheses.text: Within the same detailed occupation, renewable generation establishments pay lower mean wages than nonrenewable (fossil fuel and nuclear) generation establishments.
hypotheses.mechanism: institutional pay-setting (rent sharing, bargaining, internal labor markets) differs by technology's organizational form
hypotheses.scope: private-sector U.S. power generation, OEWS May 2021-2025

hypotheses.text: Relative to fossil fuel generation, the within-occupation gap is largest for solar and wind generation, near zero for hydroelectric generation, and non-negative for nuclear generation.
hypotheses.direction: negative for solar/wind (and biomass/geothermal); approximately zero for hydro; zero or positive for nuclear

hypotheses.text: The renewable within-occupation gap is larger in blue-collar occupational groups (construction and extraction; installation, maintenance, and repair; production) than in professional and managerial groups.

The within-occupation renewable gap does not narrow between estimates built from non-overlapping survey panels (May 2021 versus May 2024) or over May 2021-2025 (durable-inequality prediction; the ecological-modernization rival predicts narrowing).
hypotheses.direction: no narrowing (change in gap <= 0 in absolute terms)

hypotheses.text: Occupational composition does not account for the raw renewable pay disadvantage: the within-occupation renewable gap is at least as large as the raw employment-weighted gap.
hypotheses.direction: within-occupation gap magnitude >= raw gap magnitude (composition component >= 0 for renewables)

journal_calibration.theory_depth: moderate: one primary framework (relational/durable inequality) against one rival (ecological modernization), tied to just-transition debates; ~1,700 words
journal_calibration.citation_density: high in background (45-55 works), interdisciplinary mix of sociology, labor economics and energy social science
journal_calibration.must_cite_strategy: cite ERSS/energy-justice canon (McCauley & Heffron; Sicotte et al.; Burke & Stephens; Cha), closest green-wage priors (Curtis & Marinescu; Colmer et al.; Vona et al.), and wage-structure canon (Krueger & Summers; Card et al.; Tomaskovic-Devey & Avent-Holt; Western & Rosenfeld)
